newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Chirac's EMU doubts sting Italy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Chirac's EMU doubts sting Italy.

text.p: Italy responded angrily on Tuesday to doubts cast by French President Jacques Chirac on its ability to make the grade for founder membership of Europe's single currency and suggested he should stay out of Italian affairs.

The exchange set the scene for a possible clash at an Italian-Franco summit later this week and put Italy's government on the defensive over a stringent budget unveiled last Friday to try to meet the terms for joining monetary union.

"If these statements by Chirac aren't denied, we cannot but consider them as grave, grave because our country has made an exceptional effort to enter Europe," Italian deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni told reporters.
"Chirac has every right to look at the state of his own country, without interfering in the internal choices of a country which is putting together a budget," he said.
"We don't pass judgment on what others do and we expect others to act the same way."

Chirac, in a speech to businessmen in northern France, said some countries would have made the effort to "clean up their economic and financial situation" in time to join the planned launch of the "Euro" currency on January 1, 1999.
"It may take a little bit longer for those who are further behind, like Italy," he said.

Speaking in a depressed textile region, Chirac also said France had suffered from devaluations of the Italian lira, the British pound and the Spanish peseta, which had hit its textile industry harder than southeast Asian imports.
"(It is) quite obvious that the lira's movement is completely incompatible with a single European market, even if it has rebounded slightly recently," Chirac said.
Chirac is due to meet Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Thursday night and Friday in Naples for a bilateral summit expected to be dominated by monetary and economic union (EMU).

His remarks capped a painful two days for Prodi's centre-left government, which is trying to sell Italians a tougher-than-expected budget designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from the 1997 deficit.

The controversial package, almost twice as big as Prodi at first anticipated, includes provisions for a one-off "Euro tax" meant to help Italy meet the economic criteria laid down by the Maastricht treaty for membership of the single currency.

Prodi was embarrassed on Monday when Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar told the Financial Times that the Italian leader had tried to win him over to a "southern approach" to their European partners to soften the Maastricht terms.
The interview prompted an official denial from Prodi. He repeated on Tuesday that he was convinced Italy would be part of a single currency from the star .
"I knew the rules and at the right moment I have proposed figures sufficient to get us into Europe," Prodi said.
"We aren't the only ones who fear French and German competition. The French and the Germans are also very much afraid of Italian competition," he said.
"If we remain united as a country I'm telling you that we'll astound them."

Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco has also beat the patriotic drum, alleging on Monday that some of Italy's partners did not want the country in EMU. He denied on Tuesday that he had spoken of a "plot" but said the tough budget responded to a "climate in Europe aimed at excluding Italy from taking part".
